vignette: Tavita was forty-two when the chemical processing complex three miles from his West Coast home ruptured. He remembered the sky bruising purple as the containment tanks blew, the ground trembling beneath his driveway, and the immediate rush of neighbors pouring into the streets. Evacuation orders came by siren, but the air itself carried the sharp, acrid tang of spilled solvents and aged spirits from the storage warehouses the plant bordered. He spent seventy-two hours in a sheltered community center, listening to generators and the quiet weeping of families who had lost everything. The disaster left him physically unharmed but fundamentally altered. What frightened him most was not the collapse itself, but the way the event lodged in his mind, refusing to fade. Soon, his sleep fractured. He would wake from nightmares where the facility walls crumbled inward, the residue of the dream clinging to his chest long after his eyes opened. His memories of the disaster refused to blur with time; they arrived as sharp, unbroken photographs, so detailed he could count the cracked safety goggles on the ground or the exact pattern of soot on the asphalt. The images forced their way into his thoughts during quiet moments, unbidden and relentless. He found himself stopping mid-conversation, certain that the past was pressing forward. When someone asked him what he had been through, speaking the words aloud made the scene reassert itself with a clarity that left him breathless. He began to leave those questions unanswered. The scanning and the positioning occupied his hours. He learned to pull his chair close to the partition at his publishing office, always angling his back against the wall so the room opened before him. His eyes tracked every door, every sudden movement, every change in the hum of the building. Ordinary noises-a dropped stapler, the whir of a coffee maker, a phone ringing-made his shoulders jerk and his breath catch. Even in his own house, the feeling of being on guard never lifted. He kept his distance from old friends, the weight of their casual greetings feeling too heavy to bear when his mind was already crowded. When colleagues at industry mixers brought drinks, the familiar scent of alcohol on the air or on people's clothes sent a cold dread through him, and he would slip away without explanation. Over the years, the habits compounded. He stopped attending editorial reviews that required moving through crowded corridors, limiting his publishing work to email and late-night desk hours. His wife noticed how he flinched when the garage door opened too quickly, how he traced the perimeter of every room before settling in. He did not know how to explain that the past had not passed, that the images and the alertness were simply the new shape of his days. At sixty-three, what finally brought him to the clinic was a Tuesday afternoon when a sudden knock at the office door made him lurch backward, knocking his coffee onto a stack of advance reader copies. The ruined proofing remained on the desk. He drove to his first intake appointment hoping to understand why his nervous system still answered to an explosion that had happened two decades ago, and what he might do to reclaim the stillness he felt he had lost.
